title: Acid-Base Titration
subject: chemistry
description: Determine the neutralization point of an acid using a known base, watching the indicator change colour.

steps.instruction: Add 25 mL of HCl to the conical flask.
steps.hint: The acid is clear and will read a low pH on the meter.

steps.instruction: Add 3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator to the flask.
steps.hint: Phenolphthalein stays colourless in acid — that is expected.

steps.instruction: Fill the burette with 0.1M NaOH solution.
steps.hint: Record the starting volume so you can measure how much you add.

steps.instruction: Open the stopcock and add NaOH slowly to the flask.
steps.hint: Go drop-by-drop as you approach the colour change.

steps.instruction: Watch the pH meter and the indicator colour.
steps.hint: Near the endpoint the pH rises very quickly with each drop.

steps.instruction: Stop when the solution turns a faint, stable pink (the equivalence point).
steps.hint: Aim for pH 7.0 ± 0.2 and record the volume of NaOH used.

learningObjectives: Understand acid-base neutralization
Identify the equivalence point of a titration
Read a pH meter and an indicator together
Practise precise, controlled reagent addition

title: Circuit Conductivity
subject: physics
description: Build a simple circuit and discover which materials conduct electricity to light the bulb.

steps.instruction: Connect the battery to the bulb with two wires.
steps.hint: Electricity needs a complete loop to flow.

steps.instruction: Place a test material into the gap in the circuit.
steps.hint: Metals usually conduct; plastics and wood usually do not.

steps.instruction: Observe whether the bulb lights up.
steps.hint: A lit bulb means the material completed the circuit (a conductor).

steps.instruction: Swap the material and compare brightness at different voltages.
steps.hint: Higher voltage pushes more current — but watch the resistance.

learningObjectives: Understand what makes a complete electric circuit
Distinguish conductors from insulators
See how voltage and resistance affect current

title: Cell Osmosis
subject: biology
description: Observe how water moves across a cell membrane between solutions of different concentration.

steps.instruction: Place the model cell into a beaker of distilled water.
steps.hint: Distilled water has a lower solute concentration than the cell.

steps.instruction: Observe whether the cell swells or shrinks.
steps.hint: Water moves from low to high solute concentration through the membrane.

steps.instruction: Move the cell into a strong salt solution.
steps.hint: Now the outside is more concentrated than the inside — which way will water flow?

steps.instruction: Compare the cell's size in each solution and explain why.
steps.hint: Hypotonic = swells, hypertonic = shrinks, isotonic = no change.

learningObjectives: Understand osmosis across a semi-permeable membrane
Define hypotonic, hypertonic, and isotonic solutions
Predict the direction of water movement

title: Indicators & the pH Scale
subject: chemistry
description: Add acids and bases to different indicators and watch the colours map onto the whole pH scale.

HCl + Universal indicator.description: Universal indicator turns red in strong acid.

NaOH + Universal indicator.description: Universal indicator turns purple in strong alkali.

steps.instruction: Add a few drops of universal indicator to the flask of water.
steps.hint: In neutral water it should read green (pH 7).

steps.instruction: Pour in some hydrochloric acid and watch the colour.
steps.hint: Acids drive the indicator toward red.

steps.instruction: Reset, then add sodium hydroxide instead.
steps.hint: Alkalis drive the indicator toward blue/purple.

steps.instruction: Try litmus and phenolphthalein and compare their colour ranges.
steps.hint: Each indicator changes over a different pH range.

learningObjectives: Relate indicator colours to the pH scale
Compare the ranges of universal indicator, litmus and phenolphthalein
Classify solutions as acidic, neutral or alkaline

title: Precipitation Reactions
subject: chemistry
description: Mix soluble salts to form insoluble solids — watch coloured precipitates form and settle to the bottom.

Copper sulfate + NaOH.description: Pale blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate forms.

steps.instruction: Pour copper sulfate solution into the flask.
steps.hint: It is a clear, bright blue solution.

steps.instruction: Add sodium hydroxide and watch for a solid forming.
steps.hint: A pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide should appear.

steps.instruction: Rinse, then try silver nitrate with sodium chloride.
steps.hint: A white precipitate of silver chloride confirms chloride ions.

steps.instruction: Let the precipitate settle and note its colour.
steps.hint: Precipitate colour helps identify the metal ion.

learningObjectives: Understand precipitation as the formation of an insoluble solid
Identify metal ions by precipitate colour
Write the products of a double-displacement reaction

title: The Iodine–Starch Test
subject: chemistry
description: Use the classic test for starch: a milky-white suspension turns dramatic blue-black when iodine is added.

Iodine solution + Starch solution.description: Amber iodine + milky starch turns intense blue-black.

steps.instruction: Pour the milky starch solution into the flask.
steps.hint: Starch is a white, slightly opaque suspension.

steps.instruction: Add a few drops of amber iodine solution.
steps.hint: Watch the colour change immediately.

steps.instruction: Observe the deep blue-black colour that develops.
steps.hint: This colour confirms the presence of starch.

learningObjectives: Carry out the standard test for starch
Explain why iodine changes colour with starch
Recognise a positive result for a food test

title: Catalysing Hydrogen Peroxide
subject: chemistry
description: Decompose hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. A catalyst speeds it up dramatically — and some combinations are hazardous.

Hydrogen peroxide + Manganese dioxide.description: Manganese dioxide catalyses rapid decomposition into oxygen — frothy white foam and heat.

Hydrogen peroxide + Potassium permangana.description: Violent, strongly exothermic oxidation — handle with great care.

steps.instruction: Pour hydrogen peroxide into the flask.
steps.hint: On its own it decomposes only slowly.

steps.instruction: Add a little manganese dioxide catalyst.
steps.hint: Watch the oxygen froth up as white foam and the temperature rise.

steps.instruction: Note how a catalyst speeds the reaction without being used up.
steps.hint: Do NOT mix peroxide with potassium permanganate — that combination is hazardous.

learningObjectives: Understand catalysis and decomposition reactions
Identify oxygen as the gas produced
Recognise exothermic reactions and unsafe combinations

title: Metals & Acids
subject: chemistry
description: React a reactive metal and a carbonate with acid, observing effervescence, heat and the gases produced.

Magnesium ribbon + HCl.description: Magnesium fizzes in acid, releasing hydrogen and heat (exothermic).

HCl + Sodium carbonate.description: Acid on a carbonate fizzes, releasing carbon dioxide.

steps.instruction: Add a strip of magnesium ribbon to the flask.
steps.hint: The metal is solid and shiny.

steps.instruction: Pour in hydrochloric acid and watch the reaction.
steps.hint: Bubbles of hydrogen form and the flask warms up.

steps.instruction: Rinse, then try sodium carbonate with the acid.
steps.hint: Carbonates fizz too — but the gas is carbon dioxide.

steps.instruction: Compare the vigour and warmth of the two reactions.
steps.hint: Metal + acid is more exothermic than carbonate + acid.

learningObjectives: Predict the products of metal + acid and carbonate + acid reactions
Identify hydrogen and carbon dioxide gases
Link effervescence and temperature rise to reaction type

title: Projectile Motion
subject: physics
description: Launch a projectile at different angles and speeds and hit a target using real kinematics equations.

steps.instruction: Set a launch angle and an initial velocity.
steps.hint: Angle is measured from the ground; velocity is in metres per second.

steps.instruction: Launch the projectile and watch its parabolic path.
steps.hint: x = v₀·cosθ·t and y = v₀·sinθ·t − ½·g·t².

steps.instruction: Adjust angle and velocity to land in the target.
steps.hint: Range = v₀²·sin(2θ)/g — small changes near 45° matter most.

steps.instruction: Compare your attempts and find the angle for maximum range.
steps.hint: For a fixed speed, which angle sends it furthest?

learningObjectives: Apply the kinematic equations of projectile motion
Understand how launch angle and speed determine range
Discover that 45° gives the maximum range for a fixed speed

title: Forces on an Inclined Plane
subject: physics
description: Explore how weight, the normal force and friction balance on a ramp — and find the angle where a block begins to slide.

steps.instruction: Pick a surface and read its coefficient of friction.
steps.hint: Rougher surfaces have a larger μ.

steps.instruction: Slowly increase the ramp angle and watch the force vectors.
steps.hint: Weight stays constant, but its components along and into the ramp change.

steps.instruction: Find the angle where the block starts to slide.
steps.hint: Sliding begins when mg·sinθ exceeds μ·mg·cosθ, i.e. tanθ > μ.

steps.instruction: Try other surfaces and compare the slipping angles.
steps.hint: A larger μ means the block can sit on a steeper ramp.

learningObjectives: Resolve weight into components on an inclined plane
Relate the normal force and friction to the slope angle
Predict the angle at which an object begins to slide

title: Simple Pendulum
subject: physics
description: Investigate what controls a pendulum's period — length, gravity and amplitude — and confirm that mass does not.

steps.instruction: Set a string length and release angle, then watch it swing.
steps.hint: The period is T = 2π·√(L/g).

steps.instruction: Change the bob mass and observe the period.
steps.hint: Does a heavier bob swing slower? Check the timer.

steps.instruction: Change the string length and re-time the period.
steps.hint: Longer strings give longer periods (T grows with √L).

steps.instruction: Switch to Moon or Mars gravity and compare.
steps.hint: Weaker gravity means a longer period.

learningObjectives: Use T = 2π·√(L/g) to predict a pendulum's period
Show experimentally that period is independent of mass
Describe how length and gravity affect the period
Track the exchange between kinetic and potential energy
